title: A FADD-dependent innate immune mechanism in mammalian cells
abstract: Vertebrate innate immunity provides a first line of defence against pathogens such as viruses and bacteria. Viral infection activates a potent innate immune response, which can be triggered by double-stranded (ds)RNA produced during viral replication. Here, we report that mammalian cells lacking the death-domain-containing protein FADD are defective in intracellular dsRNA-activated gene expression, including production of type I (alpha/beta) interferons, and are thus very susceptible to viral infection. The signalling pathway incorporating FADD is largely independent of Toll-like receptor 3 and the dsRNA-dependent kinase PKR, but seems to require receptor interacting protein 1 as well as Tank-binding kinase 1-mediated activation of the transcription factor IRF-3. The requirement for FADD in mammalian host defence is evocative of innate immune signalling in Drosophila, in which a FADD-dependent pathway responds to bacterial infection by activating the transcription of antimicrobial genes. These data therefore suggest the existence of a conserved pathogen recognition pathway in mammalian cells that is essential for the optimal induction of type I interferons and other genes important for host defence.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2004 Nature article has had clear and durable scholarly uptake, with 288 citations and a field- and year-normalized standing in the top 10% of cited works. Its influence is concentrated in immunology and virology, where it is repeatedly taken up as a reference point for understanding FADD’s role in dsRNA-triggered innate immune signaling and interferon responses. The record also shows downstream reuse across reviews, book chapters, dissertations, and articles, along with some post-publication scrutiny in PubPeer.

Full narrative

Balachandran, Thomas, and Barber’s “A FADD-dependent innate immune mechanism in mammalian cells” helped establish FADD as more than an apoptosis-linked adaptor by connecting it to intracellular dsRNA sensing and type I interferon induction. Published in Nature in 2004, the paper sits squarely in the literature on innate immune signaling, and its citation profile shows that it became a sustained touchpoint for later work on interferon biology, pattern-recognition signaling, and cell-death pathways.

The citation landscape is broad and anchored in high-visibility venues. The work is cited most often in journals such as The Journal of Immunology, Journal of Virology, Journal of Biological Chemistry, Immunological Reviews, and Immunity, indicating that it has served both as a primary research foundation and as a synthesis point for the field. The downstream literature is not limited to research articles: reviews account for a notable share of reuse, suggesting that the paper is commonly invoked when authors summarize innate immune signaling pathways and the intersection of FADD with antiviral defense.

The topical spread of citing work reinforces that interpretation. Subsequent papers cluster around interferon and immune responses, inflammatory signaling, NF-κB pathways, and cell-death regulation, which is consistent with the article’s mechanistic reach beyond a single pathway. Recent citing papers continue to link FADD to innate immune signaling in diverse systems, including comparative and non-mammalian models, showing that the paper remains part of active mechanistic conversations rather than only a historical citation.

Beyond citations, the article has 289 documented downstream reuse events in the broader record, and scite indexes 11 supporting citation statements. Public attention is modest, with two online mentions, so the impact story is overwhelmingly scholarly rather than media-driven. The presence of four PubPeer threads indicates some post-publication discussion, but the publication record still shows strong and continuing academic uptake. Overall, this is a well-established paper whose main impact lies in shaping how innate immune sensing and FADD-dependent signaling are conceptualized across the biomedical literature.
